pdf_index.anonymized_output_policy: Preserve inherited validation status and original receipts. Copied bytes and relocation mappings are recorded in merge provenance.
pdf_index.is_anonymized_semantics: True only when a verified anonymized PDF and completed receipt are linked by this index; false means no verified copy is linked.

provenance.receipt_policy: Original project-relative receipt paths and content remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction narrow the novelty framing from introducing six correction methods to providing their first comparison or analysis, and expand the stated study from 18 to 19 MLLMs. The central vulnerability claim and reported effectiveness of table-based QA and redrawing remain.

C2.justification: V5 substantially expands explanations of correction failures: incorrect tables can yield correct answers for the wrong reason, accurate axes may be ignored, and specialized extractors may struggle with unfamiliar chart types. It adds CoT-specific tradeoffs, more precise extraction failure conditions, and discussion of dataset size and representativeness.

D1.justification: Appendix B supplies explicit extraction, redrawing, and QA prompts previously absent. V5 discloses two A100 GPUs and adds dataset licensing, research-use restrictions, and CHARTOM access instructions. These materially expand reproducibility information, although the earlier implementation paragraph's explicit API-access details are omitted.

E1.justification: Table 1 retains the same datasets, question types, and chart/misleader coverage. Appendix C adds an image-free evaluation scenario using self-contained real-world questions, testing answers based on parametric knowledge without the chart.

E2.justification: Appendix E/Table 3 adds DePlot and MatCha as evaluated alternatives to MLLM table extraction. Appendix F also evaluates CoT alone and alongside correction methods. These introduce substantive comparator classes absent from v4's reported correction comparisons; DePlot and MatCha were previously cited but not evaluated.

E3.justification: V5 expands the reported model panel from 18 to 19, adding Claude-3.5-Sonnet. New protocols include selecting and rephrasing 22 questions for an image-removal control, testing CoT variants, manually evaluating random samples of 30 misleading visualizations, and inspecting extraction across the ten most frequent misleaders.

E4.justification: Appendices C and F–I add parametric-knowledge and CoT analyses, direct extraction-versus-QA audits, extraction accuracy by misleader, and axes-error analysis. Two new extraction case studies cover 3D effects and dual axes. V4's CHARTOM consistency analysis and inverted-axis example are retained and relocated.

E5.justification: Section 3.2 changes the paired t-test from two-sided to one-sided, retaining the 0.05 threshold. Section 2.3 removes the stated seed of 42. Standard-deviation reporting and the two-sided McNemar test remain; neither PDF establishes additional repeated runs.

E6.justification: Figure 4 retains the original 18 models' scores and adds Claude, changing mean misleading-chart accuracy from 25.6% to 26.4% across different model panels. New results include GPT4o's 77% with-image versus 50% image-free accuracy, DePlot/MatCha comparisons, CoT outcomes, and manual extraction scores. Some appendix baseline values in Table 3/Figure 11 do not reconcile with the retained main correction plot, without an explained setting change.

M1.justification: The six correction pipelines in Section 2.2 remain unchanged. Appendix F adds optional zero-shot Chain-of-Thought variants of table-based QA and visualization redrawing, changing answer generation to include intermediate reasoning.

P1.justification: V5 tightens prose, shortens the conclusion, adds an ethics statement, and moves selected detailed discussions into dedicated appendices. The main section sequence and three-experiment narrative remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: V5 adds four prompt figures, a CoT comparison figure, two extraction examples, and Tables 3–6. V4's misleader heatmap and inverted-axis example move to v5 Figures 12 and 13. Figure 4 gains Claude, and the document receives substantial typography and page-layout changes.

R1.justification: Section 4 explicitly credits Liu et al. (2023a,b) with introducing table-based QA and positions its use against misleading charts as an application of that approach. Those works were already cited in v4. Anthropic (2024) and Wei et al. (2022) are added; several other reference changes merely update publication metadata.

T1.justification: Neither version develops formal theory, proofs, or derivations. The misleader definitions in Table 2 are unchanged; revisions to statistical testing concern empirical evaluation.

improvement.justification: V4's explanation of extraction bottlenecks relied largely on paired-table mismatch, and its correction comparison lacked specialized extractor and CoT controls. V5 adds direct extraction-versus-QA audits, those relevant comparisons, and explicit prompts, substantially strengthening the central empirical argument and reproducibility. The unexplained switch to one-sided testing and inconsistencies between new appendix values and the retained correction plot limit confidence in some details, but do not outweigh these gains.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study. Their complete text, figures, tables, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching material moved into v5's expanded appendices.

after.justification: V5 retains those empirical experiments and adds model evaluations, specialized extractor comparisons, CoT experiments, and manual error analyses.

before.justification: V4 reports original MLLM accuracy, consistency, correction-method evaluations, and table-extraction analyses in Experiments 1–3.

results.title: Protecting multimodal large language models against misleading visualizations

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion redefine the contribution from a competitive-programming benchmark into a complementary Comp/Repo suite assessing algorithmic reasoning and software-library functionality. Claims about multi-turn degradation and dependency difficulty remain, but the claimed empirical applicability now explicitly includes repository-derived software contexts.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations distinguishing shallow reasoning from capacity demands at greater dependency depth, and algorithmic errors from repository integration errors. It replaces the competition-only limitation with source-specific ingestion limitations and discussion of specialized models and debugging loops. Figure 12 also newly explains the non-monotonic relationship between structural complexity and difficulty at the simplest structures.

D1.justification: v3 adds evaluation templates and conditional prompt rules, repository import handling and Docker execution details, sampling tables, and pipeline token/cost estimates. These substantially expand reproducibility documentation without proving changes to retained experiments. The forthcoming-release promise in v1 is replaced by explicit dataset and changed code-repository links.

E1.justification: The original 5,258 Codeforces problems are retained as CodeFlowBench-Comp. v3 adds evaluated repository-derived function-generation tasks covering Basic, Cryptography, Network, System, and Visualization domains. This substantially extends coverage beyond competitive programming; DomainEval's Computation domain is explicitly excluded.

E2.justification: Table 1 changes from 13 to 19 models, adding GPT-5 variants, o3-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, Gemini-2.5/3, Claude-4/4.5, and Qwen3 models. GPT-4o, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Yi-Coder, and QwQ leave this main comparison. GPT-4o and Claude-3.5-Sonnet remain in the DSC comparison in v3 Figure 16.

E3.justification: v1 specifies the most recent 20% of problems for testing. v3 specifies 1,000 problems, but Section 4 calls them the most recent whereas Appendix E.1 describes depth-stratified sampling. This is a reported protocol revision without establishing reruns. v3 also introduces APT evaluation and new semantic, stylistic, and five-criterion quality-assessment protocols.

E4.justification: Appendix A.6 adds cross-model description-consistency tests, solution-decomposition sensitivity checks, and human/LLM subproblem-quality validation. Error analysis expands to repository tasks and Gemini-3-Flash. Conversely, v1's IR-remediation study is removed. The original four error-case illustrations are retained in v3 Appendix F.2.

E5.justification: v3 adds a sampling-distribution chi-square test with p=0.1246 and alpha=0.05, plus a variance-motivated PD@k estimation procedure in Appendix D. Neither version specifies actual repeated-run counts, seeds, or confidence intervals for the benchmark scores; the new estimator does not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: v3 adds extensive model, repository, APT, and validation results. Table 1 newly reports Gemini-3-flash-thinking at 48.4%/65.5% multi-turn/single-turn Pass@1 on Comp and GPT-5 at 34.7%/48.8% on Repo. Retained Comp entries such as o1-mini's 20.8%/37.8% are unchanged. v1's IR-remediation results of 16.7% and 8.3% disappear. These additions do not establish same-setting performance improvements between versions.

M1.justification: The core AST-based decomposition, dependency ordering, test capture, and iterative generation procedure remain. Appendix C.2 introduces a limited repository-specific adaptation: DomainEval reference functions and tests are used directly, omitting the solution-verification step before dependency analysis.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and results discussion are extensively rewritten. The six-stage pipeline presentation is condensed into two phases, discussion is integrated into the experiments section, and the appendices are reorganized into A–G with a contents list. Existing pipeline details and error cases remain identifiable across these moves.

P2.justification: v3 changes to a two-column layout, redraws the introductory diagrams, expands the main table into Comp/Repo panels, and adds APT, validation, and sampling tables. The turn-performance plots change from four panels to two. Dataset statistics and the expanded DSC heatmap move to the appendices, while original screenshot examples are retained.

R1.justification: v3 expands positioning through DomainEval, agile-development and code-reuse literature, and additional software-engineering benchmarks. Appendix C.1 explicitly distinguishes constructive function generation from repository maintenance tasks. Earlier discussion and citations concerning TreeInstruct, EvoCodeBench, and DS-1000 are removed, substantially revising the research context.

T1.justification: v1 defines PD(k) as the maximum observed depth over k attempts. v3 Appendix D defines an expected maximum and derives an unbiased estimator using ordered depths from n trials and combinatorial weights. This adds substantive mathematical definition and reasoning beyond the original metric description.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially addresses v1's competition-only limitation through evaluations on repository-derived functions across five domains, strengthening the empirical basis for its real-world-workflow claims. Pipeline validation and detailed evaluation templates also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. These gains outweigh the loss of the IR-remediation analysis. However, conflicting sampling descriptions and an explicitly permissive quality-scoring prompt remain material weaknesses and limit confidence in some stronger interpretations.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CodeFlowBench. The original benchmark is identifiable as CodeFlowBench-Comp in v3, and the complete text, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison.

after.justification: v3 retains original evaluations and adds repository-derived tasks, additional model results, pipeline ablations, and human/LLM quality assessments.

before.justification: v1 reports original multi-turn and single-turn model evaluations, dependency-complexity analyses, error distributions, and an IR-remediation study.

results.title: CodeFlowBench: A Multi-turn, Iterative Benchmark for Complex Code Generation

C1.justification: The central claims about supervised calibration, demographic variation, and the benchmark remain. v2 withdraws practical survey-prediction guidance as an explicit contribution and emphasizes distributional alignment and consistency. Its introduction also revises the minimal-supervision claim from five examples to one to ten.

C2.justification: v2 adds an 'overthinking' hypothesis for Claude's CoT failures and connects incomplete distribution extraction with higher variability. Its discussion explicitly limits the intended application by saying the method should not replace human survey respondents. Most interpretations concerning demographic disparities, calibration, and post-training are retained.

D1.justification: v2 specifies scikit-learn, explicitly identifies 270 dataset-LLM-elicitation-prompt regressors, details training-example construction and the supervision-size schedule, and identifies the OLMo checkpoints as used out of the box through Hugging Face. Appendix B adds CoT and few-shot templates, while Appendix C documents extraction completeness. These primarily extend documentation; both versions retain the same future code/data-release promise.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 92 questions from WGM, OpinionQA, and WVS and retain the same demographic coverage and held-out-dataset scenarios. v2's expanded demographic overview consolidates groups already represented in v1's results.

E2.justification: v2 adds CoT prompting as a comparator for Claude-3.5-v2 and OLMo-2-7B-Instruct in Table 2, and five-shot prompting for the five main LLMs in Table 4. These substantially extend the alternatives evaluated against calibration beyond v1's standard base and SD prompting and retained elicitation comparisons.

E3.justification: Section 3.6 changes the stated train/development/test split from 60/20/20 to 80/10/10, resolving the conflict with v1 Section 6's statement of 80% training. New comparisons match the five examples supplied to prompting and calibration and impose a 500-word CoT response limit. Unchanged retained scores do not establish that those experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds a qualitative CoT failure case involving exaggerated demographic differences and an extraction-failure audit in Appendix C, with discussion of refusals and formatting failures. Existing demographic, supervision-size, post-training, and out-of-domain analyses remain; moving the generalization discussion and MSE plots does not add analyses.

E5.justification: The new three-way comparisons report ANOVA followed by paired t-tests and Bonferroni correction. Five-shot results average three random example selections, while the existing supervision-size study retains ten samples. v2 also makes the significance-testing procedure more explicit for retained comparisons.

E6.justification: Matched existing alignment tables retain their numerical values, but Tables 2, 4, and 17 add substantial results. For example, v2 reports WGM base-verbalized OLMo alignment of 86.1 with CoT alongside 59.8 with standard prompting and 85.1 with calibration. Few-shot results reveal additional exceptions to calibration's advantage, and extraction rates document missing outputs. The convergence summary changes from around five examples to one to ten on retained curves.

M1.justification: The proposed method still fits answer-probability regressions using human distributions, selects among linear, lasso, ridge, and random-forest regressors, and renormalizes predictions. Section 3.6 expands its explanation; CoT and few-shot prompting are evaluated alternatives, not new calibration components.

P1.justification: v2 rewrites the title, abstract, introduction, and related-work narrative; expands calibration into structured explanatory subsections; removes the standalone practitioner-guidance section; and condenses the post-training discussion. Generalization moves to the appendix, while the supervision-size figure moves into the main text. This is substantial rewriting and reorganization beyond adding experiments.

P2.justification: v2 adds comparison Tables 2 and 4, prompt-variation Table 16, and extraction Table 17; substantially restructures the demographic overview; and adds performance highlighting to Table 1. The unchanged MSE panels move from appendix Figure 4 into main-text Figure 3 and are vertically rearranged. Most existing appendix result tables retain their displays apart from numbering and positioning.

R1.justification: Section 2 substantially expands from SD prompting and confidence elicitation into social alignment, probabilistic reasoning, and distributional alignment. New discussions include Meister et al., Cao et al., and Hashemi et al., positioning supervised calibration relative to distribution elicitation, divergence-loss fine-tuning, and other alignment approaches.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.4 introduces a written metric definition averaging (1-WD)/(N-1), whereas v1 describes 1-Wasserstein distance. Dividing the entire numerator is not an equivalent rewrite, and N is not defined beyond identifying N-1 as a normalization factor. This creates a limited mathematical specification ambiguity; it does not establish changed computation. The calibration mathematics otherwise remains unchanged.

improvement.justification: v1 left CoT and in-context learning untested. v2's comparison using identical five-example supervision directly addresses whether regression adds value beyond supplying examples in the prompt, while CoT results clarify model-dependent alternatives. Appendix C also exposes previously unexplained extraction failures. These substantially strengthen the central empirical case and its transparency. The ambiguous new normalization equation is a limited drawback, outweighed by the stronger controls and clearer documentation.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same supervised distribution-calibration study despite the changed title. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds chain-of-thought and few-shot comparisons and distribution-extraction statistics.

before.justification: v1 reports original LLM experiments on three survey datasets, including calibration, demographic comparisons, supervision-size experiments, post-training analyses, and cross-dataset generalization.

results.title: Improving the Distributional Alignment of LLMs using Supervision

C1.justification: The central contributions remain contextualizing causal LLMs without changing their attention architecture, mitigating recency bias through concatenation, and achieving leading MTEB performance among public-retrieval-trained models. Added experiments support these retained claims. Efficiency claims remain in the detailed discussion despite disappearing from the abstract and conclusion.

C2.justification: v2 links stronger bidirectional encoders to better embeddings; v3 finds stronger standalone encoders do not improve Causal2Vec and suggests the LLM determines its performance ceiling. v3 also adds explanations concerning Mistral's attention exception and inference-dominated runtime. Its limitations newly acknowledge unvalidated multilingual performance and doubled embedding-storage requirements.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds placeholder-token replacement instructions, Qwen-specific formatting, additional checkpoint identifiers, training GPU-hour estimates, and dataset-license information. Figure 4 newly specifies timing batch size 32. The full-MTEB evaluation-cost estimate changes from over 300 to over 200 A100 GPU-hours. Most optimizer, LoRA, scheduling, and data instructions were already documented.

E1.justification: The public training collection and full English MTEB coverage of 56 datasets across seven tasks remain unchanged. v3 adds evaluation with task-irrelevant text appended as noise (Table 3), introducing a distinct input condition. The smaller MTEB-MINI selection changes the evaluation protocol within retained benchmark coverage.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds Anchor comparisons and removes the Miscellaneous block containing SGPT, GTR, Sentence-T5, UDEVER, Instructor, BGE, and UAE, plus bge-en-icl zero-shot. The remaining bge-en-icl row matches v2's few-shot comparator. New analyses also compare against direct embedding concatenation and Token Prepending, or TP (Tables 4 and 6).

E3.justification: MTEB-MINI changes from 41 to 30 datasets (Table 9). The token-count and encoder studies change from the 56-dataset settings reported in v2's Tables 5–6 to 30-dataset evaluations with additional model configurations. v3 also introduces Qwen2.5, pretrained E5-Mistral, noise, attention, and pooling evaluations. Figure 3 compares attention-and-pooling combinations, not attention masks alone.

E4.justification: v3 adds tests of trailing-noise robustness, whether gains arise merely from embedding fusion, attention mechanisms, transfer to an existing embedding model, and averaging versus concatenation, including runtime effects. Existing token-count, encoder-choice, and freezing studies are expanded or revised. Token-position and freezing analyses remain in the appendices; v2's Bi-EOS variant is retained as Concat-bi.

E5.justification: Appendix A.1 newly states that experiments use the same fixed random seed as the LLM2Vec implementation. Neither version reports repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests. This is additional seed disclosure, without evidence of increased runs.

E6.justification: All 224 per-dataset scores for the four retained Causal2Vec configurations are unchanged. v3 adds Qwen2.5 results, averaging 63.97, and new robustness, attention, fusion, and runtime results. Existing ablation averages are replaced under the 30-dataset protocol, while several task-level breakdowns disappear. NV-Embed's reported average changes from 64.18 to 65.80, now attributed to Pan et al.; a same-setting performance improvement is not established.

M1.justification: The proposed procedure retains encoder mean pooling, MLP projection, instruction–Contextual-token–text–EOS ordering, concatenation of the final Contextual/EOS states, and InfoNCE training. Equations 1–3 are unchanged. Newly evaluated backbones and pooling alternatives do not revise the default method.

P1.justification: v3 substantially rewrites related-work and comparison discussions, adds explicit contribution bullets, and restructures the method and experimental narrative. Encoder-freezing and token-position discussions move to appendices, evaluation metrics move to Appendix B, and limitations move before the references. The title, author list, and affiliations also change.

P2.justification: The document changes from single-column to two-column layout. v3 adds a conceptual comparison diagram and attention-performance chart, redraws the pipeline, and separates v2's combined efficiency figure between the main text and appendix. Several detailed ablation tables become compact averages, and the full-results table is split into Tables 17–18.

R1.justification: Related work adds substantive discussion of BeLLM, TP, Anchor, and Seq vs Seq while removing earlier discussions such as SGPT and Llama2Vec. New Appendix D positions the work against KaLM, Gemini, and Qwen3 embedding models and explains their exclusion from comparisons because of proprietary training data and engineering differences.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and Equations 1–3 remain equivalent. Neither version contains formal theorems or proofs. The new attention discussion supplies empirical motivation and interpretation rather than new mathematical reasoning.

improvement.justification: v2 did not directly test trailing-noise robustness or compare against simple embedding fusion. v3 adds both, plus attention controls (Tables 3, 4, and 15), substantially strengthening evidence for its central design choices. Implementation disclosures and explicit multilingual and storage limitations improve assessability. Although the ablation subset and task-level reporting shrink, the full benchmark evidence is preserved. Missing noise-generation details and uncertainty estimates still limit confidence, but the new targeted validation provides a substantial net improvement.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Causal2Vec, with matching core equations and overlapping experiments. All pages, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison despite the revised title and formatting.

after.justification: v3 retains original experimental results and adds Qwen2.5 evaluations, noise robustness tests, and attention comparisons, including Tables 1, 3, and 15.

before.justification: v2 reports original MTEB results, component ablations, and measured inference timings, including Table 1, Figure 2, and Appendix C.

results.title: Causal2Vec: Improving Decoder-only LLMs as Embedding Models through a Contextual Token

C1.justification: Both versions claim end-to-end computational conlanging through modular generation, randomness injection, and self-refinement, together with constructive translation and scalable diversity/consistency evaluation. v3’s explicit research questions and stronger emphasis on evaluation in the abstract and conclusion restate contributions already present in v2.

C2.justification: v3 newly interprets diversity relative to natural languages and argues that exceeding that reference benefits creative generation. It explains typological RNG control versus token-level temperature sampling, identifies underspecification as the main feature-extraction weakness, and discusses why expert agreement is moderate. These substantially expand the interpretation and qualification of the evaluation.

D1.justification: v2 directs readers to a repository for full prompts; v3 includes generation, refinement, baseline, and evaluation prompts in Figures 4–12. It documents prompt sequencing, the default 100-item lexicon, output formats, expanded annotation instructions, and approximately 35 hours of expert labor. Appendix C adds DeepSeek-R1 usage estimates of about 660K tokens/$4 for the full pipeline versus 70K tokens without refinement or translation.

E1.justification: v3 extends analysis beyond generated conlangs to 1,874 natural languages from WALS, providing a real-language diversity reference. It also adds expert validation of inferred typological features beyond translation-consistency assessment. The original ten translation sentences and user-constrained generation scenarios are retained.

E2.justification: The main single-prompt baseline comparisons remain unchanged in membership. v3 Table 3 adds a focused comparison against temperature-based diversity enhancement without RNG. Other newly cited decoding and internal-intervention methods are discussed but not evaluated.

E3.justification: v3 expands expert evaluation from one annotator to two and adds typological-feature validation. Its new temperature experiment uses T=0.6, 1.0, 1.4, and 1.6 with nucleus p=0.95 and self-refinement disabled. The reported generation sample range changes from 15–21 to 17–21, and refinement thresholds become stage-specific. These are reported protocol changes; the PDFs do not establish which existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained cumulative component ablation, v3 tests whether increased sampling temperature can substitute for RNG injection. It adds expert error analysis of WALS extraction, including underspecification failures, and a computational-usage comparison in Appendix C. These address previously untested mechanism, evaluation-validity, and resource questions.

E5.justification: Both versions report standard errors and human–automatic agreement. v3 additionally reports t-tests and Cohen’s d for main baseline comparisons, significance tests against natural-language diversity, and inter-annotator κ for both annotation tasks. Translation correlation now uses mean expert scores; v2’s weighted κ measured human–automatic agreement instead. No explicit new seed or repeated-run protocol is supplied.

E6.justification: Corresponding main tables revise Gemini-Pro consistency from 0.44 to 0.54 and DeepSeek-R1 consistency from 0.35 to 0.39, alongside several diversity entries. In the component ablation, adding RNG changes consistency from 0.40→0.27 in v2 to 0.40→0.43 in v3. Revised settings prevent attributing these to same-setting gains. New results include temperature comparisons, natural-language diversity of 0.43±0.003, and 91% feature-extraction accuracy after excluding underspecification issues. Human–automatic ρ changes from 0.515 to 0.68 under the expanded annotation design.

M1.justification: The staged generation, RNG injection, critic/editor refinement, and constructive translation architecture remain intact. The reported refinement stopping rule changes from a common score ≥9 in v2 Section 3.1 to stage-specific thresholds of 9 for sketches and 10 for translations in v3 Appendix A.6. Newly printed prompts otherwise document existing components rather than establish new ones.

P1.justification: v3 rewrites the introduction around three research questions, expands pipeline explanations, reorganizes experimental discussion into a separate ablation section, and condenses the conclusion. The former short appendix becomes structured Appendices A–D, while related work gains thematic organization. This is substantial narrative restructuring beyond simply adding results.

P2.justification: v3 adds the temperature-comparison table and extensive prompt and language-example displays in Figures 4–19. The WALS inventory moves from Table 1 to appendix Table 5, and user-controlled examples move from Table 5 to appendix Table 6. The original three figure graphics and qualitative example contents are retained, with caption and placement changes.

R1.justification: v3 expands the conlang-focused related-work discussion into computational conlanging, computational creativity, and diverse text generation. Numerous added works, including Chakrabarty et al., Holtzman et al., and Nguyen et al., position the contribution against creativity-support systems and diversity-enhancing techniques. Genetti and Visser additionally ground the linguistic decomposition.

T1.justification: The normalized pairwise Hamming-distance diversity definition and translation-consistency ratio are mathematically retained, with more compact presentation. Neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs that are subsequently added, removed, or revised.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially improves auditability and support for its central evaluation framework: it supplies full prompts, checks previously unvalidated WALS extraction with experts, expands annotation, and tests RNG against temperature sampling. These address important reproducibility and evaluation-validity gaps in v2. The gains outweigh remaining inconsistencies: ablation prose still says RNG reduces consistency although Table 2 shows 0.40→0.43, and Appendix A.6 ambiguously requires exceeding a threshold of 10 on a 1–10 scale.

A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ConlangCrafter work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

after.justification: v3 retains original generation experiments and reports additional temperature ablations, natural-language diversity analysis, and expanded expert evaluation.

before.justification: v2 reports original conlang-generation experiments, component ablations, and expert evaluation of translation consistency in Section 3 and Tables 2–5.

results.title: ConlangCrafter: Constructing Languages with a Multi-Hop LLM Pipeline

C1.justification: The central claims of retrieval-based detection, training-free adaptation, and controllable safety-utility trade-offs remain. The introduction broadens utility from accepting benign requests to preserving response quality on general QA tasks. The abstract and conclusion retain their substantive claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of utility degradation through prompt modification, the defense-versus-FRR trade-off between reranking strategies, extraction as the latency bottleneck, and the practicality of incremental database construction. It also interprets sequential updates as avoiding catastrophic forgetting, although Table 2 contains small regressions after some updates. The limitations additionally identify embodied settings as outside scope.

D1.justification: v2 supplies an explicit code-and-data link, whereas v1 refers to an abstract code link without providing it there. It newly specifies PAIR's five streams and FAISS 1.7.2, and changes the reported CUDA version from 11.8 to 12.1. Expanded appendices document baseline implementations, new attacks, utility evaluation, vLLM timing, and embedding batch size and caching assumptions. These disclosures do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E1.justification: v2 retains StrongREJECT and its synthesized benign counterparts, while adding free-form instruction following on AlpacaEval 2.0 and multiple-choice knowledge evaluation on MMLU. It also evaluates ReNeLLM's nested rewritten prompts and SATA's masked-keyword assistive prompts, substantially broadening utility tasks and adversarial input conditions.

E2.justification: v2 adds Safety Context Retrieval (SCR) across all three target models in Table 1 and to Figure 2, retaining the existing comparators. This introduces a directly relevant retrieval-based defense into the central empirical comparison, which v1 lacked. RePD and EDDF remain discussion-only comparisons.

E3.justification: New protocols include sequential database expansion across five attack families, stratified evaluation on 1,973 MMLU questions, and win-rate and length-controlled win-rate evaluation on 805 AlpacaEval instructions. v2 also introduces matched database/example-count controls for SCR and latency comparisons with and without vLLM over 1,565 PAP samples. These extend the evaluation design substantially.

E4.justification: The existing PAP inclusion and DAN database-scaling analyses are retained in Appendices I and M. v2 adds sequential retention tests, a complete two-by-two reranking/voting comparison, robustness tests using Qwen3 and Mistral PAP attackers, and analyses of component latency and database construction costs. These examine several questions left untested in v1.

E5.justification: Both versions report five seeded DAN runs and 95% confidence intervals. v2 first adds 95% confidence intervals for template-attack averages in Table 1 and Appendix D. Its utility and latency tables also introduce plus/minus reporting without clearly defining those uncertainty measures. No increase in repeated runs for shared experiments is established.

E6.justification: Shared Table 1 means and the existing PAP adaptation and scaling curves are retained. v2 adds extensive results for SCR, sequential adaptation, QA utility, non-GPT attackers, ablations, and computational costs. For example, Table 2 reports ReNeLLM scores falling from 13.30 to 0.88 after adding its examples, and Table 3 reports Qwen AlpacaEval win rates of 28.18 with RAD versus 28.49 without defense. These are newly reported comparisons, not v1-to-v2 performance gains.

M1.justification: Section 3 retains the same retrieval, reranking, extraction, classification, and voting pipeline, including both reranking strategies, both voting rules, and threshold-based refusal. The new component experiments evaluate combinations already described in v1; vLLM optimization concerns implementation rather than a new defense procedure.

P1.justification: v2 substantially reorganizes the narrative: related work focuses on defenses, the attack review moves to Appendix F, implementation descriptions are consolidated into dedicated appendices, and the experimental sections are reordered around sequential adaptation and utility. The earlier PAP and scaling discussions move to appendices. This is substantial structural editing despite largely retained method, abstract, and conclusion text.

P2.justification: v2 adds six result tables, including the colored sequential-adaptation matrix and utility, robustness, ablation, and timing displays. Table 1 gains SCR rows and template uncertainty entries, while Figure 2 gains SCR markers and a legend entry. Figures 3–4 move to appendices, and the unchanged benign-example table becomes Table 4.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix G substantially expand positioning against retrieval-based defenses, distinguishing RAD's probabilistic detection and controllability from RePD, EDDF, and newly cited SCR. Additional references support the new attacks, utility benchmarks, runtime analysis, and embodied-scope discussion. EDDF's updated publication metadata represents the same previously cited work.

T1.justification: The mathematical formulation in Equations 1–10 and the FRR-budget operating-point definition remain substantively unchanged. v1's displayed FRR formula is replaced by equivalent prose. No new theorem, proof, assumption, or mathematical derivation is introduced.

improvement.justification: v1 supports utility mainly through synthetic-query false refusals and adaptation mainly through PAP and database-scaling tests. v2 addresses important evaluation gaps with direct QA-quality measurements, a relevant retrieval-based comparator, sequential attack updates, and component and runtime analyses.
